properties.name: The schema serves the TYPES and not the rules that tell them apart, and a numeric prohibition was filed as a requirement because of it
properties.source: flo2 reflow2_feedback.md, 2026-09-19 addendum (F24, F25 and the meta-point)
properties.statement:
FLO2 F24, with a measured consequence on their live site the same day: "the water can never drop below 68 degrees" was recorded as a REQUIREMENT. That is a numeric prohibition, and reflow2's own routing table sends it to a Constraint — the table even carries the near-miss in bold: 'Not a Requirement.' reflow2's own capture-intent skill says conflating the two leaves prohibitions reporting unsatisfied forever.

MEASURED 2026-09-20 on this tree. `describe_schema` answers with node types, their properties, their enums and which edges may join two types. The DISCRIMINATION RULES — the cue phrases, the near-miss each type is confused with, the counter-example — exist as a markdown table in getting-started/skills/capture-intent/SKILL.md, eleven rows, addressed to an agent reading a skill. `grep` for the rule's own words across the schema and the Rust surface finds them nowhere. So a consumer generating an extraction prompt FROM THE SCHEMA — which is exactly what the black-box rule and the toolsnaps-are-the-contract ruling tell it to do — gets six type names and none of what separates them.

⭐ THE MATERIAL ALREADY EXISTS AND IS FULLY WRITTEN. The table has cue phrases in the user's own words ('it may only be A, B or C', 'a number with a unit'), the confusable neighbour, and the routing. It is trapped in prose meant for one reader. Served as data per node type, every consumer's extraction tracks reflow2 for free — which is the whole promise of the contract being the schemas.

⚠️ AND THE SHAPE IS THE THREE-LEGS RULE AGAIN, one leg short in a new place: the typed tool exists, the instruction exists FOR AN AGENT, and the same instruction reaches no consumer building against the surface.

PRIOR ART FOUND ON A SECOND PASS, 2026-09-20, by running the root-cause skill's search step that the first pass skipped. The design already holds this ground twice over: req:a-prohibition-written-into-prose-is-noticed-as-unfiled (ACCEPTED) and cap:a-prohibition-living-in-prose-is-noticed-once-as-a-practice (REALIZED) — a detector, `prohibition_in_prose`, that scans every live Requirement, Capability, Component, Interface and accepted Decision for a prohibition that no Constraint covers, and reports it as one aggregate practice finding at severity 0.35.

⭐ SO THE OBVIOUS READING — 'reflow2 cannot notice this' — IS FALSE, AND THE MEASUREMENT SAYS SOMETHING SHARPER. The detector's vocabulary is SIX fixed phrasings. Checked 2026-09-20 against flo2's actual sentence, the one filed as a requirement on their live site: it matches NONE of the six. So the misclassification was invisible not because nothing looks, but because what looks has a closed list of six ways of saying it and the field said it a seventh way.

THAT IS A SECOND, SEPARABLE DEFECT and it belongs to the same family this project keeps meeting: a declared vocabulary that does not reach the words people actually use. The first defect — the discrimination rules are not served as data — stands unchanged and is what stops a CONSUMER from classifying correctly in the first place. The second is what stops reflow2 from noticing afterwards. Fixing either one alone leaves the other.

═══ 2026-09-22 — HALF OF THIS IS NOW RETIRED, AND IT IS DELIBERATELY NOT CLOSED ═══

THE FIRST DEFECT IS FIXED. `chg:the-schema-serves-the-rules-that-tell-the-types-apart` (merged #564) put `discrimination` on each node type in the schema — cue phrases in a person's own words, the neighbouring type and why they differ, a worked counter-example — carried through `NodeTypeSpec` so `describe_schema` serves it on both reads. Eight routed types filled in, and `tools/check_discrimination_rules.py` keeps the schema and capture-intent's table one contract. So "a consumer generating an extraction prompt FROM THE SCHEMA gets six type names and none of what separates them" is no longer true.

⚠️ AND THE ROUTING TABLE ITSELF WAS WRONG, which this finding could not have known: row 1 routed "it must never…" to Requirement while row 7 routed "we must never…" to Constraint, so the rule turned on a PRONOUN and flo2's sentence matched the wrong row. The rules had to be corrected before being served, or the defect would have been propagated to every consumer at once. Recorded as `fact:the-routing-table-contradicts-itself-and-routes-a-prohibition-to-requirement-on-the-word-it`.

🛑 THE SECOND DEFECT STANDS, UNTOUCHED, WHICH IS WHY NO `valid_to` IS SET HERE. This finding's own words: "That is a SECOND, SEPARABLE DEFECT… Fixing either one alone leaves the other." It was right. `prohibition_in_prose` still scans for six phrasings — must never, must not ever, is not allowed to, are not allowed to, never allowed, is forbidden — and CHECKED 2026-09-22, its blind spot is MODAL rather than grammatical: every one is built on MUST or ALLOWED/FORBIDDEN and none covers CAN, so "can never", "cannot", "may not" and "shall not" all miss. flo2's sentence says "can never". So the detector still cannot notice the misclassification afterwards.

⇒ CLOSING THIS WOULD ASSERT THAT BOTH HALVES MOVED. One did.
